codex.worst_flaw: The rollout rule can make the digital workflow standard based on adoption alone, without verifying that technicians still catch critical hazards after rewards end.

claude.worst_flaw: The design relies on device-captured timestamps for offline submissions to decide whether a checklist was completed before work began, but never validates or reconciles those times. Tied to a team PTO reward, this core measurement can be gamed, and the only safeguard is a generic audit.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, friction fixes, safety-hold credit, audit guardrails and a randomized stepped design are strong, but a one-hour PTO reward is modest and fairly complex to explain, so motivation and post-reward persistence depend mainly on the app fixes actually sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward rules allow inaccurate checklists to count toward paid time off, and the audit pause can miss recurring errors that keep the overall pass rate within five percentage points of baseline.

claude.worst_flaw: The all-or-nothing 75% crew threshold for paid time off can create peer pressure on technicians with difficult jobs. The design names no check for that pressure, no rule for crews with few eligible jobs, and no clear rule for jobs that are late or missed. It also has no sample-size or uncertainty plan for the paired two-wave comparison.

holistic.reason: Co-designed with stewards, protects safety holds, bans punitive data use, and has a randomized stepped rollout with clear decision thresholds, but the crew-based 75% threshold risks peer pressure and rushed or backdated entries, and a single paid hour may not be a strong enough hook to make the habit stick once it's withdrawn.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew reward pays only after a crew reaches 70%, so a few low-adopting technicians can block it for everyone, which creates peer pressure; the design never addresses this, its pilot comparison uses few crews and has no power or spillover analysis, and the event and audit trail stays thin, with appeals handled only through the existing support channel.

codex.worst_flaw: The 70% crew payout threshold has no demonstrated feasibility and makes earned time off depend partly on app failures and differences in assigned visits.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, a paid-time reward, safeguards against pressure to start unsafe jobs, and a pre-set decision rule make it approvable, but a 6-week crew reward delivered through a weekly briefing may not catch attention, and the 70% post-reward bar is a stretch from 35% today.

claude.worst_flaw: Payout settlement depends on a single rota owner correcting counts from the PR record with no replayable policy versions, shadow validation or independent appeal, while the quality pause depends on existing review-quality checks or defect triage that may not detect shallow approvals within the reward window.

codex.worst_flaw: With only one review group per condition in the two-week comparison, the pilot cannot reliably distinguish the reward’s effect from differences between groups.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with team-wide reward, no individual pressure, workflow fixes, a quality guardrail and a staged-rollout evaluation, but it is complex for skeptical engineers, and a half-day prize plus measurement overhead may feel heavy, with lasting change depending on whether the default workflow sticks.

codex.worst_flaw: The clock starts only after assignment, so ready PRs can wait indefinitely for a reviewer while the reported on-time rate still meets the target.

claude.worst_flaw: Quality relies on existing maintainer follow-ups and incident reviews rather than an independent sample audit, and there is no separate tracking of whether complex PRs wait longer, so rushed approvals and cherry-picking could go unnoticed; corrections are also handled by private message with no appeal path or replayable event history.

holistic.reason: It fixes the review queue before offering any reward, uses a shared team goal with no rankings, and has a randomised stepped rollout, but it is complex to run and relies on one review lead and an unvalidated 'substantive' judgement.

claude.worst_flaw: Operability is thin: one engineering lead privately fixes disputed counts with no event history, independent validation or separate appeal path, and the substantive-review spot check (5 reviews per retro) is too small and owned by the same person who runs the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: A documented hold earns full credit without verification that anyone takes the stated next step, so the pilot can reach 80% while substantive reviews remain delayed.

holistic.reason: It fixes the queue first, uses a low-stakes team lunch, keeps managers and performance reviews out, and builds in a phased comparison and gaming checks. But the lunch is a weak lever, a few details (80% target, 8-hour clock, spot-checking) add some complexity, and engineers may not care much about it, so the lasting effect depends mostly on the queue and rotation changes staying in place.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot uses observed sessions to decide whether routine logging has improved and persisted, with no specified way to detect whether nurses log more often when an observer is present.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never checks whether kiosk logging of hand-hygiene moments adds clinical value over the existing observer audit, and its learning design (one randomly early ward, a two-week gap, observer-dependent verification with no replayable event history) cannot tell a reward effect apart from Hawthorne effects or ward differences.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with paid trial time, no individual surveillance, pause rules, gaming checks and a drop rule, but a ward-level catered meal is a weak, delayed motivator that nurses may barely notice, and the habit may fade once rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The adoption measure blocks launch because the design does not specify how to link kiosk entries to distinct eligible nurse shifts before aggregating them for the 80% threshold.

claude.worst_flaw: Its core pilot signal is unreliable: the reward depends on one monthly observer audit per ward (a small, Hawthorne-prone sample), there is no replayable event record, shadow validation or staffed appeal, and the kiosk adoption measure rewards one entry per shift rather than the accuracy or completeness of logged moments.

holistic.reason: Rewarding audited compliance rather than self-logged entries avoids gaming, and the pause rules and staggered start are sensible, but a one-off shared meal for three wards is a weak, easily forgotten incentive, and the kiosk logging has no points or strong pull to sustain it after the offer ends.

claude.worst_flaw: Because the meal is ward-level and verified only by a small monthly observer sample, a few observed moments decide the reward, and there is no replayable event or policy versioning, independent shadow validation or staffed appeal path beyond the infection-prevention lead's corrections.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward is not launchable until auditors can verify that each anonymous receipt corresponds to one specific observed hand-hygiene opportunity and cannot earn credit twice.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, safety-conscious pilot with verified outcomes and harm pauses, but the ward-level meal reward is a weak, delayed signal, the audit-sample verification is complex, and its lasting effect rests mainly on the simplified workflow.

codex.worst_flaw: The paid-time-off threshold treats unchecked ticket records as correct, so irrelevant links and unsupported exceptions can earn credit whenever they fall outside the QA sample.

claude.worst_flaw: The all-or-nothing 80% reward threshold over a four-week window does not handle small or zero-opportunity caseloads, and the team-randomised comparison with only a few teams has no plan for uncertainty or case mix.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with exceptions, QA, guardrails, randomized stagger and clear decision rule, but a single hour of paid time off is a modest reward and the long, multi-part mechanics may dilute attention, with habit retention depending mainly on the workflow fixes rather than the reward.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait until the design specifies how QA findings affect paid-time-off qualification, since irrelevant links and invalid exceptions could help a team reach its target while failures stay below the pause threshold.

claude.worst_flaw: The design gives every member of a team an hour of paid time off only if the whole team hits its target, and it removes valid exceptions from the article-rate denominator, which creates peer pressure and a motive to inflate exceptions; the QA sample may be too small to catch this, and the few randomized teams leave the incremental-lift estimate underpowered, while there is no replayable event log and appeals go only to the support lead.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, QA guardrails, a CSAT pause rule and a staggered evaluation, but the team-wide paid-hour reward, exception loophole risk and complexity for a 60-person org may limit uptake, and gains could fade once rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The primary metric is a launch blocker because valid exceptions can raise the score above 60% even if agents link or write no more articles on tickets that need them.

claude.worst_flaw: The design leans on the operations lead editing disputed counts directly in the ticket record. It has no versioned event or policy history, no independent shadow validation and no staffed appeal path. On top of that, the four-week staggered pair comparison, with only a few teams, is too small to separate the reward's effect from noise, and the design doesn't plan for that uncertainty.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with workflow fixes, a gaming-resistant disposition rule, QA checks, CSAT guardrails and a staggered comparison, but it is complex to run, a team-level 60% target with one hour off is a modest, weakly visible reward, and the 'not needed' exception plus a 60% target jump from 12% make gaming and a fade-out after rewards end real risks.
